meta.title: Conflict Watchlist
meta.notes: Fully automated register: a scheduled open-source review rewrites this file daily (procedure in docs/WATCHLIST-REVIEW.md) and an hourly GitHub Action refreshes the live reporting feed (watchlist-live.json) from GDELT. Every comparison the dashboard shows (state moves, changed dimensions, the attention-score bonuses) is made against the register as it stood compareDays (7) days ago, taken from each item's `snapshots` (one entry per review: date, state and the five dimensions). Each review: (1) set reviewDate/previousReviewDate, (2) for every item set the new `now` on the five dimensions and the new `state`, then append today's snapshot (keep the last 60), (3) rewrite `status` (`summary`: plain-language current status whose first sentence states the newest development; `sources`: 2–3 links to the newest reporting), `whyNow`, `topic` and `whyMatters` (stable framing, revise only on a phase change), `changes` (dated bullets covering the last 7 days: keep those still inside the window, add today's, drop older ones), `next`, `ignore` and `sources`, (4) record any state move in `history` and keep `timeline` (4–8 dated one-line events of the current phase, chronological) current. The dashboard derives attention rank, movements, changed-dimension flags, staleness, coverage surges — do not type those in. `next` holds named, checkable indicators.

1.desc: High relevance to the Army — followed every week in the brief.

2.name: Active Regional & Escalation Watches

Priority.desc: Direct strategic relevance or high Army learning value.

Active.desc: Material trend, escalation, or regional relevance.

Watch.desc: Baseline monitoring; no current learning priority.

Archive.desc: Reserve — retained for reference and pattern work; revisit only on a named trigger.

phase.label: Conflict phase
phase.desc: A short label for the stage the conflict is in (for example attritional war, ceasefire without implementation, grey-zone contest). It sits under the current-status summary and shows the label from 7 days ago when it changed.

escalation.label: Escalation risk
escalation.desc: How likely a step up in intensity or a change of phase is in the coming weeks.

levels.Low: Stable; no live trigger and restraints hold.
levels.Moderate: Triggers exist (deadlines, disputes, incidents) but restraints are holding.
levels.High: Active exchanges or a named trigger that is likely to fire; a phase change is plausible within weeks.
levels.Severe: Active war or ongoing kinetic exchange with strategic stakes (major shipping lanes, energy, great-power forces).

tempo.label: Operational tempo
tempo.desc: How much military activity is actually happening in the review window.

levels.Medium: Recurring incidents or steady, limited operations (patrols, fortification, occasional strikes).
levels.High: Daily strikes or operations across fronts.

adaptation.label: Adaptation behaviour
adaptation.desc: How much new tactical or technical behaviour appeared in the window; this is where the Army learning sits.

levels.Low: Both sides are using the same methods as before.
levels.High: Novel, repeatable adaptations appeared (new weapons employment, counter-measures, doctrine shifts).

sgExposure.label: Singapore exposure
sgExposure.desc: How directly the conflict touches Singapore's interests. Not shown as a register column; it still feeds the attention score and the expanded row.

levels.Moderate: An ASEAN or diplomatic role, observer contributions, or supply-chain spillover.
levels.High: Direct effect on sea lanes, energy or shipping, a Singapore-flagged vessel affected, or relevance to deployments.

attentionScore.desc: Deterministic, explainable rank. state (Priority 40 / Active 25 / Watch 10 / Archive 0) + escalation risk (Severe 20 / High 15 / Moderate 8 / Low 2) + 5 per dimension that changed over the last 7 days (compareDays) + 10 if the state moved up over the same window + Singapore exposure (High 8 / Moderate 4 / Low 0) + tier (T1 6 / T2 3 / T3 0) + 8 if the live open-source feed shows a coverage surge (see definitions.feed.surgeRule). Items flagged ignore-for-now are shown but ranked last.

feed.source: GDELT DOC 2.0 API (open, no key). Per item: 30-day daily article counts (TimelineVolRaw) and the most relevant English-language articles of the last 7 days (ArtList, HybridRel). Synced by .github/workflows/sync-watchlist-feed.yml into watchlist-live.json.
feed.surgeRule: A coverage surge is flagged when the last 7 days carry at least twice the article volume of the 7 days before and at least 20 articles; a surge adds 8 points to the attention score.
feed.titleFilter: Articles are kept only when the title contains one of the item's terms, to cut GDELT's full-text noise.
feed.terms: Title filter: at least one of these substrings must appear in an article title for it to count as reporting on the item.
feed.require: Optional groups of substrings; a title must contain at least one term from every group (two-party theatres: one term per side).
feed.exclude: Optional substrings that drop a title (sport, entertainment and other noise), in addition to the sync's global list.
feed.spamDomainsNote: Article sources dropped outright (livestream/score spam). The daily review adds domains seen producing noise.

columns.tier: Standing relevance to the Army: T1 Priority Conflicts, T2 Active Regional & Escalation Watches, T3 Baseline Regional Research Reserve. Tiers do not change week to week.
columns.state: Today's monitoring state: Priority (direct strategic relevance or high Army learning value), Active (material trend, escalation or regional relevance), Watch (baseline monitoring), Archive (reserve; revisit on a named trigger). ▲▼ marks a move over the last 7 days.
columns.status: Current status: the newest title-matched headline from the live open-source feed (synced hourly) on top, then a plain-language summary of what is happening now whose first sentence states the newest development, with links to the newest reporting it rests on. The phase label sits beneath; a struck-through label is the phase 7 days ago.
columns.coverage: Open-source coverage from the live feed (GDELT with Google News fallback): the sparkline is the last 30 days (or four weekly counts), the number is articles in the last 7 days with the change against the 7 before. 'Surge' = at least twice the prior week and at least 20 articles. Refreshes hourly.
columns.nextIndicator: The soonest dated indicator to watch, tagged with the numbered topic and watch area it informs (or 'cross-cutting' when it bears on the theatre as a whole). Expand the row for the full list.
columns.confidence: How well-sourced the assessment is: High (multiple independent, dated sources), Medium (some single-source or snippet-only items), Low (thin or contested reporting).
columns.attention: Attention score, the register's sort order. Hover a score for its breakdown.
columns.topic: Topics of interest: the three capability contests the Army follows this theatre for, set by the team (from the watchlist workbook). Numbered so they line up with the 'Why it matters' and 'Watch areas' columns; the chip is the topic's adaptability rating.
columns.whyMatters: Why it matters here: for each numbered topic, what the theatre tests (the capability, behaviour or mechanism under study).
columns.watchAreas: Watch areas: for each numbered topic, its watch status and what to monitor. Status tags: Rising (activity increasing), Established (steady pattern), Contested (the outcome is still open), Watch for trigger (review only on a named event), Background monitor, Declining.
columns.adaptability: Adaptability: how transferable the topic's lessons are to the Army — High, Medium or Low, set by the team.

infoOps.desc: Information operations and strategic communications watch. Switched on for an item when a trigger event (a summit, a crisis) makes messaging and influence activity worth tracking on its own: a narrower hourly feed of reporting on official messaging, state-media narratives and documented influence campaigns, plus dated findings and an assessment researched daily from open sources.

types.official statement: Government, foreign-ministry, military or party statement aimed at an audience (strategic communications).
types.state-media narrative: Framing pushed by state or party media, including English-language outlets aimed abroad.
types.covert information operation: Documented coordinated inauthentic behaviour, disinformation or cognitive-warfare activity, attributed by a credible reporter.
types.coercive signalling: Military, coast-guard or legal action whose purpose is the message it sends.
types.sanctions/lawfare: Sanctions, lists or legal framing used to pressure or delegitimise.
types.counter-messaging: The targeted side's official response or rebuttal.
types.domestic narrative: Narratives inside the targeted polity (parties, polls, viral claims).
types.debunked claim: A specific false claim identified by a fact-checker.
types.third-party assessment: Analysis by a think-tank, researcher or major outlet.

phase.now: Attritional stalemate; reciprocal deep-strike war; US pushing a trilateral technical round while Ukraine holds local initiative north of Lyman

items.whyNow: Diplomacy and the deep-strike war are running on parallel tracks: on 25 Sep Kyiv and the Kremlin both confirmed a US proposal for technical-level trilateral talks (UAE mooted) and Putin said every peace proposal stays on the table, yet the same day Russian drones killed seven in Kyiv, Putin promised 'retaliatory strikes' for Ukraine's election-week attacks, and Ukraine's General Staff confirmed hits on the Lukoil Perm refinery 1,450 km from the border, a second refinery, two radars and a missile-component plant, while Macron calls a 300,000-strong Russian mobilisation 'plausible' and Poland raises its air posture.
changes: 25 Sep: Russian drone attacks on Kyiv through the night and day killed seven people including a 14-year-old boy in a 16-storey Pecherskyi block and four at an office building in Solomianskyi, with 57 injured by 8 p.m. (Ukrinform, Kyiv Independent); the same day Zelensky said the US had proposed technical-level three-way talks, possibly in the UAE, and awaited a date, and Peskov said a trilateral meeting could happen soon (Al Jazeera).

25 Sep: Ukraine's General Staff confirmed overnight strikes on the Lukoil-Permnefteorgsintez refinery (13 Mt/yr, about 1,450 km from the border), the Novoshakhtinsk refinery (7.5 Mt/yr), a 64L6 Gamma-S1 and a 39N6 Kasta-2E2 radar near Novoshakhtinsk and the Iskra plant in Ulyanovsk (semiconductors, Kh-59 and Pantsir components); Russia's MoD claimed 592 drones intercepted and governors reported one killed in Perm, eight injured in Ulyanovsk and 13 in Voronezh, where the Voronezhsintezkauchuk plant was hit (Ukrinform, Meduza, Moscow Times).

25 Sep: Putin said all peace proposals remain on the table but Russia must weigh its interests, that Moscow had been ready to resume talks after the 18–20 Sep Duma vote until Ukraine attacked Moscow and polling stations ('they should be made to feel Russia's retaliatory strikes'), and that Russia is not preparing military action against Europe; Bloomberg reported Trump had urged Zelensky on 22 Sep to meet Putin in Moscow and been refused, which the Presidential Office denied, saying only trilateral talks were discussed (Kyiv Independent, Al Jazeera, Meduza).

25 Sep: Zelensky said Trump told him in New York he had made a 'final decision' to grant Ukraine Patriot missile production licences, two days after the State Department told DW no final decision had been made (Kyiv Post); Macron on 24 Sep called reports that Russia is preparing to mobilise a further 300,000 men 'plausible', citing 'several signs' (Meduza); Poland's defence minister raised F-16 and helicopter activity after the 23 Sep Mi-8 incursion, Tusk warning parliament of planned Russian hybrid drone and missile strikes on states backing Ukraine (Al Jazeera).

24 Sep: Russia's night attack with 282 drones, four Zircons and three ballistic missiles killed 16 and injured 59 across Ukraine and damaged a maternity hospital and energy sites; Peskov said Moscow seeks 'peace, not a temporary ceasefire' after Lavrov on 23 Sep ruled out any pause during talks; ISW's 24 Sep assessment recorded no advance by either side and called Russian claims of encircling Dobropillia cognitive warfare unsupported by battlefield evidence; suspected Russian drones crashed in Romania and Moldova (Kyiv Independent, ISW via Kyiv Post, New Voice of Ukraine).

20 Sep: Operation Vivaldi phase two retook Shandryholove, Derylove and Drobysheve north of Lyman, the 3rd Army Corps crediting ground robots with 15,700 missions and 90% of frontline evacuations (single source); on 25 Sep Zelensky reported 'positive news' near Lyman but said the operation is not over (Kyiv Independent, Defence Matters, Ukrainska Pravda, single source).

next.text: Date and venue of the US-proposed technical-level trilateral round confirmed by Kyiv and the Kremlin on 25 Sep (UAE mooted); whether it opens with a limited energy-strike moratorium on the table after Lavrov (23 Sep) and Peskov (24 Sep) rejected any pause.
next.ifSeen: Round convened with an energy moratorium on the agenda → phase check and flag this week; round slips past October → expect the winter energy campaign to open unchecked.

next.text: Putin's 25 Sep 'retaliatory strikes' line translated into a repeat of the 24–25 Sep pattern: two or more raids of 250+ drones with ballistic waves on Kyiv in a single week, or a strike package against gas production and heating plants before the heating season.
next.ifSeen: Escalate; the ballistic interception rate over Kyiv (60% on 24 Sep) becomes the metric for layered defence.

next.text: The Patriot production licence Zelensky said on 25 Sep Trump had 'finally' approved put in writing (DSCA notification or a Raytheon/Ukrainian partner announcement), and the 24 Sep interceptor deal made public.
next.ifSeen: Confirmed → note for the monthly pattern set on sovereign interceptor production; denied by Washington again → track only.

next.text: CEC final Duma results (due by 5 Oct) followed by a Russian mobilisation decree or covert call-up of the 300,000 Macron called 'plausible' on 24 Sep, or Ukraine's own mobilisation changes enacted.
next.ifSeen: Decree → escalate and phase check; no decree but regional call-up orders → monthly pattern note on force generation under attrition.

next.text: Vivaldi phase three toward the Zherebets line after Zelensky's 25 Sep 'not over' remark, or a Russian shift south toward Sloviansk; any verified Russian advance toward Dobropillia against ISW's 24 Sep finding of no progress.
next.ifSeen: Phase check: attritional stalemate versus an operational-level shift.

next.text: Further NATO airspace incidents after the Mi-8 over Poland (23 Sep) and drone crashes in Romania and Moldova (24 Sep); a NATO shoot-down over Poland under the raised posture announced on 25 Sep, an Article 4 consultation, or the hybrid strike on a supporter state Tusk warned of.
next.ifSeen: Alliance-response dimension → escalate if a shoot-down or consultation occurs.

next.ifSeen: Tightening confirmed → sustainment pressure on Russian refining compounds Ukrainian strikes; track repair times at struck refineries.

timeline.text: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held three-hour talks with Vladimir Putin in Moscow, then travelled to Kyiv under a three-day pause on strikes against both capitals.
Russia hit Kyiv with 32 cruise missiles and 166 Shahed-type drones, over half jet-powered, killing five and ending the pause declared during the US envoys' visit.
Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps revealed Operation Vivaldi, a counteroffensive near Lyman it said cleared 75 square kilometres of Russian infiltrators and liberated Serednie and nearby villages.

A Ukrainian drone strike set both crude distillation units ablaze at Gazprom Neft's Moscow refinery, followed on 22 September by strikes on the Ufa and Samara refineries more than 900 kilometres from the border.
Zelensky met Trump at the UN General Assembly, said Ukraine is ready for a reciprocal energy ceasefire, and urged trilateral talks with Putin at the G20 in Miami.

After meeting Rubio in New York, Lavrov said Russia would not pause its military operation during negotiations in any format, while Peskov said the next day that Moscow seeks peace rather than a temporary ceasefire.
Russia launched 282 drones and three waves of ballistic and Zircon missiles, killing 16 people across Ukraine including two in Kyiv, while suspected Russian drones crashed in Romania and Moldova.

Russian drones killed seven people in Kyiv as Ukraine's General Staff confirmed strikes on the Lukoil Perm refinery 1,450 kilometres from the border, and Kyiv and the Kremlin both confirmed a US proposal for technical-level trilateral talks.

text: On persistent ISR versus signature management and deception, the Established and Contested status is borne out tactically and contested in the information space. The 3rd Army Corps’ 20 Sep account of Vivaldi credits ravine approaches and search-and-strike drone teams for surprise north of Lyman, Zelensky on 25 Sep called the operation unfinished (single source), and ISW on 24 Sep read Russian claims of encircling Dobropillia as cognitive warfare. Deception works for one corps; scaling it is unproven. On EW versus alternative UAS control and layered counter-UAS, the Rising rating holds and the pressure has shifted to mass and launchers: the 24 Sep raid mixed 282 drones with Zircon and Iskander waves and killed 16 despite 227 downed, drones killed seven more in Kyiv on 25 Sep, and Ukraine’s answer is industrial, the Patriot production licence Zelensky said on 25 Sep Trump had approved.

On contested sustainment versus dispersed support and repair, the Established and Contested status is borne out on both sides. On 25 Sep the General Staff confirmed hits on the Perm and Novoshakhtinsk refineries, two air-surveillance radars and the Iskra component plant, while Russia struck Kyiv energy and logistics on 24–25 Sep. Endurance now turns on refinery repair times, radar replacement and the 300,000-man mobilisation Macron called plausible on 24 Sep; the corps’ claim that robots ran 90% of evacuations (single source) shows where dispersed support preserves tempo.

phase.now: Ceasefire without implementation; Yellow Line creep and targeted strikes

items.whyNow: The truce's first anniversary approaches with targeting, not implementation, setting the tempo: on 25 Sep the IDF said it has now killed 16 'key' Hamas financial officers and will keep going, a strike at the gate of a displacement camp in al-Mawasi killed another Palestinian, two reservists died when their own Atalef FPV drone exploded in the northern buffer zone, forcing the IDF to ground all small explosive drones, and WHO's Tedros told UNGA that Gaza still faces a public health emergency, while Hamas demands entry of the technocratic committee and the ISF that Mladenov says run to no timetable.
changes: 25 Sep: An Israeli strike on a civilian vehicle at the gate of the Wijdan displacement camp in al-Mawasi, Khan Younis, killed one Palestinian and injured several (Arab News, WAFA); the IDF said two reservists of the 7007th Battalion, Nadav Kali and Ofek Moalem, were killed on 24 Sep when an Atalef FPV drone crashed on take-off inside a post in the northern buffer zone and exploded as they picked it up, and it grounded all small explosive-carrying drones pending a brigadier-general inquiry that will examine Hamas electronic interference, which the IDF assesses Hamas lacks the capability for (Times of Israel, JNS).

25 Sep: The IDF and Shin Bet said they have killed 16 'key' Hamas financial officers who moved more than $1bn to the military wing through dozens of money changers in Turkey and Gaza, and warned they will 'continue to act' against the financing mechanism (Times of Israel); WHO Director-General Tedros told UNGA that Gaza 'continues to face a humanitarian and public health emergency' nearly a year into the ceasefire and called for medical supplies, facility rehabilitation and expanded medevac (ANHA, single source); a new KSrelief aid convoy entered Gaza (SPA).

25 Sep: The New York Times corroborated Haaretz's report that UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed warned Netanyahu of a 'major attack' by Hamas about a week before 7 Oct 2023 in a 45-minute call, and that Netanyahu did not raise it with security chiefs on 1 Oct while telling them Gaza strikes could harm Saudi normalisation; Netanyahu's office denies any such call (Haaretz, Times of Israel). Hamas dismissed Netanyahu's UN speech as 'lies and slogans' (Palestinian Information Center, single source) and Kallas said Gaza progress is 'far too limited' (Anadolu).

24 Sep: Netanyahu told the UN General Assembly that genocide allegations are 'the biggest lie of the century' without setting out ceasefire steps; Hamas spokesman Hazem Qassem said the movement is 'fully ready' to implement the Board of Peace roadmap, demanded entry of the technocratic committee and deployment of the international force, and accused Israel of 'complete obstruction' and Mladenov of failing to compel it (CBS, Jerusalem Post, Middle East Monitor).

24 Sep: Mladenov told a UNGA side event the Board is 'not working according to a timetable' and Maj-Gen Jasper Jeffers outlined area-by-area demilitarisation with a permanent 5,000-person Rafah ISF site (Jerusalem Post, single source for the figures); UNCTAD put recovery needs at $71.5bn (Al Jazeera); an Israeli strike on a vehicle at al-Baidar killed one man and a second strike hit the vehicle carrying his body (WAFA, Arab News); the health ministry put the toll at 73,928 since October 2023 and 1,408 killed since the ceasefire (TRT World).

23 Sep: The Board of Peace unveiled a $2.4bn, 66-project six-month reconstruction plan conditioned on Hamas disarmament, the same day an Israeli strike in western Khan Younis killed Hamas finance chief Mohammad Abu Elwan among seven killed (Al Jazeera, Jerusalem Post); on 22 Sep Katz ruled out any partial withdrawal from the 63% the IDF holds until full disarmament (Jerusalem Post).

timeline.text: The UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2803, endorsing the US Gaza plan, welcoming the Board of Peace and authorising an International Stabilization Force for Gaza.
Israel's security cabinet approved entry of an initial International Stabilization Force of about 200 personnel from countries such as Uganda and Morocco, operating in coordination with the IDF.
Hamas approved the Board of Peace's plan pairing gradual disarmament with phased Israeli withdrawal, a plan Netanyahu rejected pending genuine disarmament.
An Israeli-backed raid in Gaza City detained the head of Hamas's internal security service; airstrikes covering the withdrawal killed at least five Palestinians, including two children.
UN humanitarian officials said Israel had pushed the yellow line inward, leaving Palestinians under 40 percent of Gaza, with 1,334 killed since the ceasefire.

The Board of Peace unveiled a $2.4bn, 66-project reconstruction plan conditioned on Hamas disarmament, while an Israeli strike in western Khan Younis killed senior Hamas finance official Mohammad Abu Elwan among seven dead that day.

Netanyahu told the UN General Assembly that genocide allegations are the biggest lie of the century, while Hamas said it was fully ready to implement the roadmap and demanded entry of the technocratic committee and deployment of the international force.

The IDF said it had killed 16 key Hamas financial officers and would keep targeting the financing network, and grounded all small explosive drones after two reservists were killed by their own FPV drone in the northern buffer zone.

text: On dense urban operations versus dispersed and concealed networks, the Established and Contested status is borne out by a shift in method: the IDF said on 25 Sep it has killed 16 financial officers who moved over $1bn via Turkish and Gazan money changers, after finance chief Abu Elwan’s death on 23 Sep, so the network is now attacked through its cash flow rather than its tunnels. The 24 Sep death of two reservists from their own Atalef FPV drone, and the grounding of all small explosive drones, shows the cost of drone-centric buffer-zone operations. On persistent ISR and precision strike versus civilian protection and legitimacy, the Contested status is confirmed: a vehicle was struck at a displacement-camp gate in al-Mawasi on 25 Sep, 1,408 have died since the truce, and on 25 Sep the New York Times corroborated the UAE pre-7 Oct warning Netanyahu denies, so targeting freedom carries a rising legitimacy cost.

On humanitarian access versus operational control, the Established status holds and access remains a lever: Katz on 22 Sep ruled out withdrawal from the 63% the IDF holds before full disarmament, Mladenov on 24 Sep said the $2.4bn plan runs to no timetable, Hamas demanded the technocratic committee and ISF be let in, and Tedros on 25 Sep said Gaza still faces a public health emergency (single source). Entry control, not capacity, governs endurance into winter.

changes: 25 Sep: FM Araghchi told reporters at the UN that Iran has given Washington a 'concrete' seven-day plan (halt to operations on all fronts including Lebanon, lifting of the naval blockade, oil-export waivers, sanctions relief and unfrozen assets, with the strait open 'at the end of the seventh day' and talks restarting) and that the choice now rests with the US; a senior Iranian official told Reuters Tehran will make no nuclear concessions even if the plan is accepted and the strait stays closed until 'all of Iran's conditions are met'; Rubio said it would be wrong to call the contacts a breakthrough and Trump said 'I think we're going to do great' (Reuters via Yahoo/US News, Al Jazeera, CNBC).

25 Sep: A US official told CBS the New York talks were 'positive and constructive' but Washington was 'not in a rush' given its advantage over the strait; CENTCOM said nearly 40 million barrels of crude moved through Hormuz under US escort in the past two days and that the blockade had redirected seven vessels in two days, 122 since 14 July; Iranian technical experts joined the New York discussions (Al Jazeera via CBS); a US official counted about 60 commercial transits on 24 Sep with the highest daily crude volume since early July, while The National counted 13 Hormuz crossings that day (CBS News, Baird Maritime, The National).

25 Sep: Baghdad, Najaf, Erbil and Sulaimaniyah airports suspended all Iranian flights under US secondary sanctions on air-service providers, following the UAE, Qatar, Azerbaijan and Georgia; supreme leader's adviser Mohammad Mokhber said flights in the region are 'either free for everyone, or for no one'; Brent fell about 2% to $104–105 and WTI to about $92 on the diplomacy (Al Jazeera, Ynetnews, CNBC, The National).

25 Sep: Three Iran-linked tankers seized in the Indian Ocean in April and June (Tifani, Majestic X, Lenore) are crossing the Atlantic toward US ports with about 4 million barrels of Iranian crude worth roughly $600 million for forfeiture in the Southern District of Texas; SNSC secretary Rezaei separately gave Washington four to five days to accept Iran's conditions 'completely and all at once' (gCaptain, Bloomberg, Gulf News).

24 Sep: Reuters sources said US and Iranian negotiators were exploring a staged deal in which Iran reopens Hormuz and Washington lifts the economic blockade; the Senate failed 49–50 to advance the Iran war-powers resolution; Brent settled at $106.60 after a $108.23 high on the Houthi barrage at Saudi Arabia (Reuters via Yahoo, CNBC, NPR).

23 Sep: Iran handed the US a written road map through Qatari, Pakistani and Egyptian mediators; the bulk carrier Cape Dao was hit by an unknown projectile off Musandam with one seafarer killed; Rezaei warned neighbours enforcing US aviation sanctions that their own airports would not operate (The National, gCaptain, Jerusalem Post).

timeline.text: The US and Iran signed a 14-point memorandum of understanding that lifted the US naval blockade, reopened the Strait of Hormuz and opened a 60-day negotiating period.
After Iranian strikes on vessels collapsed the June ceasefire, US Central Command resumed its naval blockade of Iranian ports and struck Iranian anti-shipping targets near Hormuz.
US strikes on Iranian coastal radars killed 11 people, including five at a wedding in Kuhestak; the IRGC answered with missile and drone attacks on US bases in Bahrain, Jordan, Iraq and Kuwait.
After the IRGC fired anti-ship ballistic missiles at a US carrier and destroyer, CENTCOM destroyed or disabled three Iranian tankers, the Downy, Stark 1 and Kylo.
Witkoff and Kushner held three hours of Qatari-mediated indirect talks with Iran's foreign minister in New York, as Trump told the UN he could 'annihilate' Iran absent a deal.

Iran handed the US a written road map for a 60-day regionwide ceasefire, phased reopening of Hormuz and an end to the blockade, while the bulk carrier Cape Dao was hit off Musandam and one seafarer was killed.

Reuters reported US and Iranian negotiators exploring a staged Hormuz-for-blockade deal, hours after the Senate failed 49–50 to advance a resolution to end the war and Rezaei threatened neighbours' airports over US aviation sanctions.

Foreign Minister Araghchi put a 'concrete' seven-day plan to Washington to end hostilities, lift the blockade and reopen Hormuz before nuclear talks, a senior official ruled out any nuclear concessions, and Iraq's four airports cut all Iranian flights under US sanctions.

text: On long-range strike versus integrated air and missile defence, the Established · Contested watch area stayed quiet on the direct axis through 25 Sep: no coalition strikes on Iranian soil and no IRGC launches at Gulf hosts were reported, and the test of Saudi interceptors on 24 Sep came from Iran's Houthi partner. Coercion has moved to the aviation layer: after US secondary sanctions closed Iraqi, Emirati and Qatari airports to Iranian carriers on 24–25 Sep, Rezaei and Mokhber threatened that no regional airport would operate, an airspace-denial tool that air defence cannot answer. On maritime chokepoint disruption versus energy-route resilience, the Established · Contested status is borne out but the evidence is split: the Cape Dao was hit on 23 Sep, yet CENTCOM said on 25 Sep that nearly 40 million barrels moved under US escort in 48 hours, while Bloomberg counted ten commodity vessels and The National 13 crossings on 24 Sep. Resilience rests on escorted convoys and rerouted Saudi barrels, and Araghchi's seven-day plan makes reopening a sequenced bargaining asset.

On deterrence versus proxy and deniable escalation, the Rising · Contested status holds: unattributed sea strikes on 21 and 23 Sep, Houthi barrages that Pezeshkian disowned on 24 Sep and Iran's refusal on 25 Sep to concede on enrichment even if its plan is accepted show layered pressure running alongside talks, keeping adaptability High.

changes: 25 Sep: PM Nawaf Salam told the UNGA general debate Lebanon wants Israel to withdraw 'from all Lebanese territory up to our internationally recognized borders', its detainees released, 'weapons held by the state alone' with war-and-peace decisions reserved to constitutional institutions, and that 'no one speaks on behalf of Lebanon, and no one negotiates for it' but the state, framing the US-mediated talks with Israel as the route to end the war (Al Jazeera; Israel National News; Haaretz). US Ambassador Michel Issa said Hezbollah handing over its weapons 'would pave the way for peace' (L'Orient Today, single source).

25 Sep: Israeli airstrikes hit Bani Hayyan, the Kfartebnit–Nabatieh al-Fawqa area, the outskirts of Zawtar al-Sharqiyeh and the valley between Froun and Ghandourieh, artillery shelled Zawtar al-Sharqiyeh, Mayfadoun, Nabatieh al-Fawqa, Wadi al-Hujeir, Majdalzoun and Kfartebnit, homes were set alight in Khiam and a mass detonation was carried out at Deir Seryan near Taybeh; no casualties were reported and the Health Ministry toll since 2 Mar stays at 4,386 killed and 12,407 wounded (Naharnet; Al Jazeera). The 8,953-dead figure circulating on 25 Sep is the ministry's cumulative count since 8 Oct 2023, published 17 Sep, not a new toll.

25 Sep: The IDF fired an interceptor at a 'suspicious aerial target' over the area where its troops operate in south Lebanon and said within hours that an initial assessment showed a 'false identification', with the incident under review; no Hezbollah launch was claimed (Times of Israel liveblog; Israel National News). Hezbollah MP Hassan Fadlallah said Hezbollah and Amal are 'not against a political solution' and open to indirect negotiations that lead to liberation of the south, 'not through surrender', and that no reasonable solution has been offered since 27 Nov 2024 (Naharnet).

24 Sep: Overnight Israeli artillery hit Beit Yahoun, Shaqra, Kounine, Hadatha and Mansouri, airstrikes hit Mayfadoun, Mansouri, Qantara, Wadi al-Hujair and Wadi Slouqi, and a large detonation was set off around Bint Jbeil, the second night of demolitions after Khiam (Naharnet; Middle East Monitor). On the UN sidelines Salam proposed a Security Council-mandated monitoring and liaison presence to avoid a vacuum after UNIFIL, told Iran's Pezeshkian Lebanon will not be 'a stage for regional conflicts', and Netanyahu told the UN Hezbollah's leaders are dead (Arab News; UPI; Times of Israel).

23 Sep: An Israeli mass detonation at Khiam blacked out Hasbaya, Shebaa and Arqoub and shattered windows in a Marjayoun school, followed by white-phosphorus shelling of Wadi Zebqine, Baraashit, Zawtar al-Sharqiyeh and Mayfadoun (Naharnet, single source); Hezbollah's Mohammad Raad said the group held Ali al-Taher for four months to foil the framework's implementation mechanism, and Macron told the UN France will support a replacement for UNIFIL (Naharnet).

18–22 Sep: Israeli tanks forced the Lebanese army off a new post outside Deir Mimas that Israel said lay inside its Yellow Line, a Hezbollah roadside bomb lightly wounded two Israeli soldiers inside the zone, and UNIFIL counted nearly 30 Israeli military positions in south Lebanon including eight fortified bases (Naharnet; Arab News; Times of Israel; The National).

Prime Minister Salam told UN sideline meetings that Lebanon wants full Israeli withdrawal and a Security Council-mandated international presence to avoid a vacuum after UNIFIL, as Israeli artillery, airstrikes and a second night of demolitions continued across the south.

Salam told the UN General Assembly that Israel must withdraw to the recognised borders and that weapons must be held by the state alone, while Israeli strikes, shelling and a mass detonation at Deir Seryan continued and the IDF fired an interceptor over the zone at what it later called a false identification.

text: On border-zone security versus rocket, drone and dispersed-launch threats, the Established and Contested reading holds. Israeli fire came daily from 23 to 25 Sep, with strikes across Nabatieh district on 25 Sep and mass detonations at Khiam, Bint Jbeil and Deir Seryan, while no Hezbollah rocket or cross-border launch was reported; the last acknowledged Hezbollah action is the 19 Sep roadside bomb, and the 25 Sep interceptor fired at a false identification shows a hair-trigger inside the zone. Raad’s 23 Sep claim that Hezbollah held Ali al-Taher to foil the framework mechanism (single source) and Fadlallah’s 25 Sep line that indirect talks are acceptable but ‘not through surrender’ show attrition and negotiation running together. On precision strike versus escalation control, restraint is contradicted at the edge: the Khiam blast on 23 Sep blacked out Hasbaya, Shebaa and Arqoub (single source) and at Deir Mimas on 18 Sep the Yellow Line was enforced by tanks against the Lebanese army.

changes: 24–25 Sep: PM Anutin Charnvirakul told the UNGA general debate on 24 Sep (New York) that Thailand and Cambodia have 'navigated a difficult period', that Thailand 'has never sought conflict' and 'is engaging in good faith', that he and Hun Manet had agreed in May to settle border issues bilaterally but Cambodia instead launched compulsory UNCLOS conciliation, which he stressed concerns maritime delimitation only, and he urged Phnom Penh to work on joint border security, demining and dismantling online-scam networks (Thai PBS World; Nation Thailand; Bangkok Post; Khaosod English). Cambodian analyst Nhel Rattha called the remarks 'a diplomatic tactic and the creation of a political narrative' (Phnom Penh Post, single source); no official Cambodian reply or podium statement by Prak Sokhonn had appeared by run time.

25 Sep: The Aviationist published mission markings on 19 RTAF F-16s of the 103rd and 403rd Squadrons at Korat showing Mk.82, Mk.84, Lizard/GBU-12 and KGGB employment in the July and December 2025 operations, one airframe carrying 16 Mk.82 icons, with T-50TH and F-5TH aircraft also marked; December targets included the Chai Chum Neang bridge complex (13 Dec) and sites in Preah Netr Preah and Poipet (15 Dec) (The Aviationist, single source). No border incident was reported on 25 Sep.

24 Sep: Thailand's Joint Information Center chief ACM Prapas Sornchaidee urged Hun Manet to implement Clause 10 (anti-scam and trafficking cooperation) of the 27 Dec 2025 agreement and to measure results in networks broken and victims rescued (Nation Thailand; Straits Times via Asia News Network). Sihasak said the second UNCLOS round in The Hague 'will move on to the substance' and Prak Sokhonn called conciliation 'a means to rebuild trust, not a form of escalation' (Thai PBS World; Khmer Times).

23 Sep: At the International Conference on Combating Online Scams in Phnom Penh, Hun Manet said anti-scam efforts 'should not be used as a tool to attack other countries or as a pretext for military force' (Nation Thailand; Asia News Network).

22 Sep: Cambodia lodged a formal protest over a Buddha statue placed by Thai troops and monks on 18 Sep at Phnom Beng, Anlong Veng, between border posts 2 and 3, calling it another 'fait accompli' on occupied land (The Star / Phnom Penh Post; Kiripost).

18–25 Sep: No exchange of fire, drone crossing or mine casualty was reported; the only military-technical items in the window are Cambodia's 15 Sep protest of a Thai trench near Boundary Pillar 9 and the 17 Sep Hill 450 trench settlement by liaison (Khmer Times; Khaosod English, single source).

items.whyNow: Rodríguez's UN week has turned into a legitimacy harvest: after her 23 Sep pledge of elections without a date and her first meeting with Trump, Chile's Kast and Trinidad's Persad-Bissessar have both re-opened relations, and a 25 Sep Foreign Policy read is that Washington will not press for a vote. Machado remains blocked in Panama after seven failed returns and is weighing a public, escorted attempt, the 24 Sep Caracas march demanded a 2027 election, and the maritime strike campaign has paused since the 70th strike on 19 Sep (234 dead).
changes: 25 Sep: Nothing new on the military track: no JTF-WHEM strike or interdiction since the 70th strike on 19 Sep (Just Security timeline, checked 25 Sep). The day's reporting was diplomatic and legal: Foreign Policy summarised Rodríguez's UN debut as a legitimacy win, noting the Trump administration is working with her on oil while declining to press for elections and that Latin American presidents are normalising with her (Foreign Policy); Barbados Today reported Venezuela's joint communiqué with Trinidad and Tobago (below); and SDNY prosecutors' opposition to Cilia Flores's bail request was reported, arguing 'extreme flight risk' and possible witness intimidation, with the joint Maduro–Flores trial set for 1 Jun 2027 (De Último Minuto, single source; Miami Herald headline in feed).

24 Sep: Rodríguez and Trinidad and Tobago PM Kamla Persad-Bissessar met at Venezuela's UN mission and issued a joint statement calling it 'the beginning of a new era in bilateral relations', pledging cooperation on trade, energy, security, disaster risk management and air connectivity and reciprocal visits, and Venezuela declared Persad-Bissessar 'persona grata', reversing the October 2025 National Assembly declaration under Maduro (Barbados Today; Nation News; CNC3). Machado's team is reported to be considering an openly announced return escorted by international figures instead of discreet routes (CiberCuba citing NTN24, single source).

24 Sep: Hundreds of opposition supporters marched from Plaza Venezuela to the National Electoral Council in Caracas demanding Machado's safe return, new CNE authorities and a presidential election in 2027, with no security-force response reported (EFE via Infobae; La Nación). Machado's team said three attempts to leave Panama on 21–22 Sep failed, seven blocked returns in all; Trump and Rubio denied a US hand (MercoPress; UPI).

23 Sep: Rodríguez told the UN General Assembly 'elections will be held in Venezuela' at a moment the people will decide and thanked Trump for restoring cooperation (Al Jazeera; UPI). Chile's President Kast met her in New York and proposed restoring ties 'paso a paso', consular matters first, saying Venezuela must recover its institutional and judicial processes; El Nacional dates the meeting 24 Sep (Meganoticias; El Nacional; Venezuelan presidency).

22–23 Sep: Rubio said the Trump–Rodríguez pull-aside covered restructuring about $60bn of defaulted bonds; the IDB president is drafting a two-year engagement plan centred on electricity and social protection and working on a $2.5bn loan needing waivers against board pushback (Reuters via US News; Reuters via Investing.com).

18–21 Sep: CNN reported MQ-9 Reapers moving from Africa to SOUTHCOM for anticipated counternarcotics operations; Halliburton signed non-binding agreements with Eneva and WESCA on 21 Sep; the 70th boat strike on 19 Sep killed four, bringing the toll to 234 (CNN; World Oil; SOUTHCOM).

timeline.text: US forces captured President Nicolás Maduro and his wife in overnight strikes across Caracas and three other states, flying them to New York to face narco-terrorism charges.

Trump held a pull-aside meeting with interim President Delcy Rodríguez at a UN General Assembly reception, their first encounter since Maduro's capture, covering debt restructuring; the same day Machado's team said three attempts to leave Panama for Venezuela had failed within 24 hours, her seventh blocked return.

Addressing the UN General Assembly, Rodríguez pledged elections and a transition to 'full democracy' and said dialogue with the opposition had opened, but gave no date; Chile's Kast met her the same week to begin restoring consular ties.
Hundreds of opposition supporters marched from Plaza Venezuela to the National Electoral Council in Caracas demanding Machado's return, new electoral authorities and a presidential election in 2027.

Venezuela declared Trinidad and Tobago's prime minister persona grata after she and Rodríguez agreed at Venezuela's UN mission on a 'new era' of cooperation in energy, security and trade, reversing the 2025 persona non grata declaration.

text: On counter-criminal operations versus sovereignty and escalation, the trigger has not fired: US action stays at sea, the only new military move is the MQ-9 shift to SOUTHCOM reported on 18 Sep, and no strike followed the 70th of 19 Sep. On border and maritime control versus illicit networks, the Established status is borne out at a lower rate: two Caribbean strikes in September (9 and 19 Sep, seven dead) against the earlier weekly pace, with no reported spillover.

On information operations versus political legitimacy, the Rising status is borne out and the balance tilts toward the interim government. Rodríguez pledged elections at the UN on 23 Sep without a date, a day after meeting Trump; Chile's Kast agreed on 23 Sep to restore ties step by step, Trinidad's Persad-Bissessar signed a 'new era' communiqué on 24 Sep and was declared persona grata, and Foreign Policy's 25 Sep read is that Washington will not press for a vote. Against that, Machado's team said on 24 Sep that seven returns have been blocked and is weighing an escorted public arrival (single source), and hundreds marched to the CNE on 24 Sep demanding a 2027 vote with no security response. Legitimacy is drawn from Washington and regional capitals on one side and the street on the other; adaptability stays Medium, the calendar rather than force being the contested ground.

findings.text: A Global Times English editorial on 25 Sep 2026, closing out coverage of Xi's state visit, called Taiwan 'the most important and sensitive core issue in China-US relations' and repeated Xi's hope that the US will 'uphold the correct stance of opposing Taiwan independence'. It aimed Beijing's summit line at foreign readers.

findings.actor: PLA (per ROC Ministry of National Defense)
findings.text: In the 24 hours to 06:00 on 25 Sep 2026, covering summit day, Taiwan's MND reported only 2 PLA aircraft sorties, 6 PLAN ships and 5 official ships, down from 10 sorties a day earlier. Air pressure dropped sharply while Xi was at the White House, though naval presence continued. An independent tracker also recorded 2 sorties and 11 vessels on 25 Sep.

On 25 Sep 2026 Taiwan's Foreign Ministry rejected Xi's White House remarks as Beijing's 'consistent approach of distorting facts', said the ROC and PRC 'are not subordinate to each other', and called China the 'true disruptor' of regional peace. This was a same-day rebuttal of the Chinese readout in which Xi urged the US to 'uphold the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence'.

On 25 Sep 2026 the MAC said the CCP 'repeatedly propagates its Taiwan position through US-China dialogue' to link Taiwan to 'constructive strategic stability', and that such stability cannot be a pretext for annexation. It also rebutted Xi's WWII 'fought side by side' framing, saying the PRC did not exist until 1949 and that the ROC was America's wartime ally.

On 25 Sep 2026 KMT chair Cheng Li-wun said Taiwan 'does not need to choose' between being pro-US or pro-China while Washington and Beijing pursue their own interests. She urged President Lai to present concrete proposals to lower Strait risk and restore cross-strait communication.

On 25 Sep 2026 Atlantic Council's Markus Garlauskas said no public Taiwan bargain emerged, but Taiwan is not 'unaffected' because the arms package is still pending. Josh Lipsky judged the summit an optics win for Beijing because its near-equal 'G2' framing showed Washington standing 'toe to toe with China' rather than leading a coalition.

findings.actor: Wall Street Journal (as reported by China Times)
findings.text: On 25 Sep 2026 China Times reported a WSJ editorial warning that a US shift from 'not support' to 'oppose' Taiwan independence would let Beijing weaken Taiwan's confidence in US support and justify more pressure. The editorial reportedly argued that Trump's May 'negotiating chip' remark encouraged Xi's demand. (single source; WSJ original not opened)

According to the PRC MFA readout of the 24 Sep 2026 White House talks, Xi told Trump that China's position on reunification is 'clear-cut' and that the US should 'adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence' and 'handle the Taiwan question with caution'. This goes beyond the long-standing US 'do not support' wording. On 25 Sep, Taiwan's MOFA rejected it as 'distorting facts and unilaterally conveying its own positions'.

On 24 Sep 2026, Xinhua English ran an 'Urgent' flash saying Xi hopes the US will oppose 'Taiwan independence' and handle Taiwan 'with prudence'. Trump and Xi would not tell reporters whether Taiwan came up, and the White House had issued no readout by that night, so Beijing's version was the only public account of the Taiwan exchange.

A China Daily editorial on 24 Sep 2026 said the US 'must handle the Taiwan question ... with extra prudence and caution'. It called the one-China principle, the three communiques and 'commitments made by previous US administrations' 'international obligations', framing US arms support for Taiwan as a breach of those commitments.

findings.actor: PLA (per ROC Ministry of National Defense)
findings.text: In the 24 hours to 06:00 on 24 Sep 2026, as Xi arrived in Washington, Taiwan's MND detected 10 PLA sorties, 6 PLAN ships and 6 official ships. Five of the sorties crossed the median line into Taiwan's northern and central ADIZ.

On 24 Sep 2026 Trump called the talks a 'great meeting' but declined reporters' questions on Taiwan, and Xi also did not answer. The White House had issued no readout as of that evening, leaving Xinhua's account of Xi's Taiwan demands as the only official version.

On 24 Sep 2026 Cabinet spokesperson Michelle Lee said the government 'maintains close communication with the US' at all levels. She pointed to the existing Taiwan-US trade and investment frameworks as the government's answer to talk of trade-offs over arms and tariffs. (single source)

On 24 Sep 2026 UDN reported that Taiwan's national-security team had war-gamed the summit. Unnamed NSB officials said the US had stressed 'publicly and through private channels' that its Taiwan policy is unchanged, and that Beijing views delaying arms sales as the 'first brick' of a US retreat from the first island chain. (single source)

A Global Times editorial on 23 Sep 2026, published as Xi's visit began, put 'the Taiwan question' first among Beijing's 'four red lines' that 'must not be challenged'. It said the US must 'handle the Taiwan question with utmost prudence'.

On 23 Sep 2026 an unnamed Taiwanese national security official said Beijing uses think-tank reports and academic papers to push the narrative that the first island chain is a burden and that the US should 'abandon Taiwan'. The official also said Beijing labels Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines as regional 'troublemakers' and offers 'empty promises' such as soybean and LNG purchases and delayed arms sales. (single source)

assessment.text: Sources for 21 to 26 Sep 2026 show a Beijing-led strategic-communications effort that uses the summit itself as its main channel. The White House issued no readout by 24 to 25 Sep and Trump declined Taiwan questions, so Xinhua's account of Xi urging Washington to 'oppose Taiwan independence' stood as the only official record (Taipei Times, Focus Taiwan, 25 Sep). US messaging was divided, not coordinated with Beijing. On 23 Sep Rubio kept the arms package 'under review', while Republican senators and House members from both parties publicly objected. No September count of coordinated inauthentic activity was found. The NSB's May baseline (about 100 account groups, more than 9,000 posts; Taipei Times, 26 May) is the latest quantified reference, so any post-summit campaign is unmeasured. Taipei answered quickly across agencies. On 25 Sep MOFA and the MAC rejected Xi's framing and his WWII 'ally' narrative, and the Cabinet, MND and NSB stressed continuing US contact. At home, the 21 Sep poll (47% doubtful) and the KMT's 25 Sep call for cross-strait talks show that abandonment narratives already find receptive ground.

22–23 Sep: Trump's UNGA speech called Sharif a 'terrific man' and again claimed credit for ending the May 2025 war, which India denies; India signed a Rs 810.79 crore contract for 160 satellite-guided Smart Anti-Airfield Weapons, deliveries 2027–29 (Dawn; The Week).

timeline.text: A Hague Court of Arbitration unanimously rules the Indus Waters Treaty remains fully in force and bars India from raising the Ratle dam; India rejects the award within hours as 'illegally constituted'.
Pakistani troops fire small arms and mortars across the Line of Control in Poonch's Mankote sector, a day after firing in Krishna Ghati; the Indian Army retaliates.

Indian destroyer INS Kolkata and Pakistani patrol vessel PNS Hunain collide in the North Arabian Sea during Pakistan's SEASPARK-26 exercise, the first physical military incident since May 2025, and each side summons the other's charge d'affaires the next day.
Two Pakistani Jaish-e-Mohammad militants are killed overnight in 'Operation Sohan' in the Majalta forests of Udhampur, Jammu, and a suspected over-ground worker is detained.
India rejects Pakistan's version of the warship collision as 'the usual prevarication', insisting INS Kolkata was on routine surveillance in international waters.

Dar tells the OIC Contact Group in New York that the Indus treaty is binding and cites the August award, India rejects the group's Kashmir communiqué, and New Delhi signs a contract for 160 satellite-guided anti-airfield weapons.

India's envoy at the UN Human Rights Council tells Pakistan that 'neither terror nor theatrics' will repay its loans and demands it vacate the parts of Jammu and Kashmir it holds, as New Delhi restates that the Indus arbitration court is illegally constituted.

Sharif tells the UN General Assembly that any attempt to stop, impede or divert Pakistan's share of the Indus waters 'will be treated as an act of war', calls Kashmir Pakistan's 'jugular vein' and credits Trump's intervention in the May 2025 conflict, while an Indian diplomat shakes his head in the hall.

text: On cross-border strike and counterstrike versus escalation management, the Established · Contested status held without a kinetic test: after the 15 Sep Arabian Sea collision both navies settled into competing narratives, the last move being India’s 18 Sep rebuttal, and the only Line of Control reporting between 18 and 25 Sep was three mines defused in Poonch on 23 Sep. Signalling has moved to hardware and exercises: the 23 Sep contract for 160 anti-airfield glide bombs and Tarang Shakti at Jodhpur from 26 Sep with six US F-35As keep India’s stand-off airfield-strike option visible. On counterterrorism versus interstate deterrence, the Established rating rests on words: India’s 24 Sep UNHRC reply tied Pakistan to ‘exporting terror’ and no attack followed the 17 Sep Udhampur encounter.

On air, missile and information operations versus nuclear-threshold ambiguity, the Contested edge sharpened on 25 Sep when Sharif told the General Assembly that any diversion of Pakistan’s Indus share ‘will be treated as an act of war’ and again credited Trump with ending the May 2025 fighting, which India answered only with a diplomat’s head-shake pending its right of reply. The red line is conditional on a diversion India has not begun, so it hardens the information contest rather than the military one; adaptability stays High but unexercised, the window’s adaptations being India’s lawfare and stand-off munitions against Pakistan’s declared casus belli.

changes: 25 Sep: Malaysia's foreign minister Mohamad Hasan told the OIC ministers' meeting at UN headquarters that a Rohingya solution 'must address its root causes, including citizenship status' and reaffirmed support for The Gambia's ICJ case, while NST headlined a Malaysian call for Myanmar to fulfil the Five-Point Consensus; Bangladesh's Coast Guard seized 48 tonnes of urea (960 sacks) being loaded on a fishing boat for Myanmar at Mirsarai, a day after a 30-tonne seizure at Sitakunda (Bernama; NST headline only; The Daily Star).

25 Sep: Junta attacks on villages near the 115-Mile rest stop on the Yangon–Mandalay expressway in Bago killed seven and drove more than 1,000 people to Taungoo; junta forces and a Rawang militia are abducting villagers and IDPs as porters and conscripts in Putao and Khaunglanhpu, northern Kachin; the regime banned TIME and blacklisted its editor over the 23 Sep Min Aung Hlaing interview in which he urged Washington to 'review [sanctions] objectively' and promised a democracy fitting Myanmar's 'culture, customs and traditions' (Myanmar Now; BNI; DVB; DMG).

24–25 Sep: Junta jets bombed the NUG's Special Military Region headquarters near the Mon–Bago border in Kyaikto (KNU Brigade 1 area) at about 11:00 on 24 Sep, followed by artillery from Thein Za Yat and reconnaissance drones that blocked rescue; IMNA counts at least four dead, Myanmar Now six including a CDM ex-Air Force sergeant, Mizzima/BNI at least ten (figures conflict); an Air Force strike on a truck rest stop at Sattawkone, Indaw, killed two civilians (IMNA; Myanmar Now; BNI; DVB).

24–25 Sep: A Delhi court allowed Matthew VanDyke and six Ukrainians, on bail since 18 Sep over alleged drone training and drone imports for Myanmar ethnic armies, to leave India for a month, resolving last run's custody conflict; four Tangkhul Naga civilians were shot dead near Pilong, Kamjong district, between border pillars 91 and 93, with Kuki National Army-Burma cadres crossing from Myanmar blamed by local sources and a 24-hour Naga shutdown following (Militarnyi; India Today NE; Deccan Herald) (attribution unverified).

25 Sep (reported): Heavy clashes near Kangyi village and Point 948 on the Thahpanyaung–Talaingtaung corridor from 20–23 Sep killed two LID 55 battalion commanders, Lt-Cols Tin Myo Htut and Myat Thin Kyaw, as the junta push from Mindon into Ann stalled under Arakan Army fire and retaliatory jet strikes; the regime has blocked the corridor road linking Rakhine to central Myanmar (BNI/NMG) (single source, casualties unverified). The 1,000-troop DDI 25 column in Saw Township has not moved on Mindat or Kanpetlet.

24 Sep: Myanmar recalled its ambassador to Thailand for questioning over migrant trafficking and visas for anti-regime figures (Thai PBS World, citing The Irrawaddy) (single source); Malaysia will deport a first batch of 1,476 Myanmar migrants on 29 Sep, with Anwar inviting Min Aung Hlaing for an official visit; junta kamikaze drones have killed 20-plus civilians in Karenni since early September (Myanmar Now; DVB; BNI).

timeline.text: Min Aung Hlaing is inaugurated as president of Myanmar's quasi-civilian military government in Naypyitaw, and on 21 April offers armed groups peace talks with a 100-day deadline that the KNU, CNF and NUG reject.
The military launches 'Operation 4926', a combined land, naval and air offensive against the Arakan Army across Sittwe, Ponnagyun, Kyaukphyu and Gwa townships in Rakhine State.
Six fibre-optic FPV drones strike Tada-U airbase near Mandalay; resistance says Yak-130 jets were hit, the junta says all were intercepted, and international flights are cancelled.
The Arakan Army's counter-offensive seizes four junta outposts on the Sittwe-Ponnagyun border, including positions near Minchaung Bridge and the Shwe Min Gan naval station.

A junta column of over 180 vehicles and about 1,000 troops with MLRS, drones and signal jammers reaches the DDI 25 weapons plant in Saw Township to renew the offensive on Mindat and Kanpetlet in southern Chin State.
An Air Force strike on a truck rest stop at Sattawkone village on the Mandalay-Myitkyina highway in Indaw Township kills two civilians and destroys two trucks.

The Arakan Army repels a two-week junta attempt to breach the Maei mountain pass at Mindon into Rakhine, Malaysia sets a 29 Sep date to begin deporting Myanmar migrants after Anwar invites Min Aung Hlaing for an official visit, and Myanmar recalls its ambassador to Thailand for questioning.

Three junta jets bomb the National Unity Government's Special Military Region headquarters in Kyaikto near the Mon–Bago border, killing between four and ten resistance personnel, as a Delhi court lets the American and six Ukrainians accused of drone training for Myanmar insurgents leave India.

text: On distributed resistance versus state airpower, the Established · Contested status holds and airpower keeps substituting for ground movement that fails: the Mindon-to-Ann push cost LID 55 two battalion commanders between 20 and 23 Sep (single source), the Maei pass attempt was repelled by 24 Sep (single source), and the 1,000-troop column at DDI 25 has not moved on Mindat or Kanpetlet. The regime’s answer was jets: three bombed the NUG’s Special Military Region headquarters at Kyaikto on 24 Sep, artillery and reconnaissance drones then denied rescue, and attacks near Bago’s 115-Mile rest stop killed seven on 25 Sep. On commercial UAS and improvised systems versus conventional advantage, the Rising status is borne out on both sides: the junta now pairs strike with drone overwatch, and the 24 Sep Delhi order letting the American and six Ukrainians leave India confirms the Mizoram–Chin drone-training pipeline was real and is tolerated.

On fragmented governance versus logistics and civilian resilience, the Established status is confirmed by neighbours shaping the corridors: Bangladesh’s 24–25 Sep urea seizures (78 tonnes in two days) show Rakhine’s farm supply running through smuggling, the 24 Sep Kamjong killings blamed on Myanmar-based Kuki cadres (attribution unverified) reopen the Manipur border, and Malaysia’s 25 Sep root-causes line at the OIC precedes its 29 Sep deportation flight. Adaptability stays High; the transferable lesson is drone-enabled denial of rescue after a strike.

items.whyNow: On 25 Sep Yemen's President al-Alimi declared general mobilisation and offered Houthi defectors amnesty from 26 Sep, the Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani chiefs of staff met in Riyadh and agreed to deepen military and intelligence cooperation and integrate defence capabilities under the Makkah pact, UNICEF said 130,000 people including 71,000 children were displaced in three weeks, and Pakistan's PM told the UN that any attack on Makkah is a 'red line' and Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab must stay open. Government forces are holding the Kahboub heights and taking positions in Lahj, France's Yanbu detachment is pending, Bab al-Mandab saw 27 crossings on 24 Sep, and coalition forces in Iraq are down to Erbil airport before the 30 Sep exit.
changes: 25 Sep: Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council chair Rashad al-Alimi called for 'general mobilisation and national mobilisation' behind the armed forces and offered a general amnesty to Houthi fighters and affiliates who quit the group from 26 Sep; the vice-president said the Houthis use shipping security 'as a tool for blackmail' (France 24, Anadolu, Arab News, Al Jazeera).

25 Sep: The Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani chiefs of staff met in Riyadh under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement and agreed to deepen military and intelligence cooperation and integrate defensive capabilities, without announcing deployments; Erdogan said support could take the form of intelligence, logistics or ammunition; Houthi official al-Bukhaiti warned Pakistan and Turkey of an 'iron fist' if they join; PM Sharif told the UNGA that any threat to Makkah or Madinah is a 'red line', condemned the Houthi attacks and said Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab must remain open (Arab News, Al Jazeera, Dawn).

25 Sep: UNICEF said about 130,000 people, among them 71,000 children, were displaced in three weeks, mostly from or within Taiz, the worst wave since the 2022 truce; more than a quarter of 2,900 screened children were acutely malnourished, 243 schools closed and at least 15 children killed since early September; Iraq's Baghdad, Najaf, Erbil and Sulaimaniyah airports suspended all Iranian flights under US aviation sanctions (Al Jazeera, Arab News).

25 Sep: Government forces (Nation's Shield, Giants Brigades, Al-Sabiha tribesmen) took Jabal Nouman and other positions on the Al-Sabiha front in Lahj after holding Kahboub for almost a week against repeated Houthi assaults, with the Houthi offensive described as stalled; Houthi probes toward Hayjat al-Abd and al-Maqatirah on the Taiz–Aden road were repelled (Arab News, Ibrahim Jalal brief, single source for the road probes); no new Houthi launches at Saudi Arabia were reported on 25 Sep after the six ballistic interceptions of 24 Sep (Al-Monitor).

24 Sep: The Houthis fired ballistic and cruise missiles and drones at Jazan, Yanbu, Taif and Riyadh, the coalition intercepted six ballistic missiles aimed at Taif and Yanbu, Macron said France will send soldiers, radars and defence systems to protect the Yanbu terminal, and the Makkah-pact foreign ministers met in New York; Brent hit $108.23 before settling at $106.60; The National counted 27 Bab al-Mandab crossings that day (Anadolu, France 24, Arab News, The National).

24 Sep: Coalition forces in Iraq are present only at Erbil airport ahead of the 30 Sep exit, with militia disarmament moved to June 2027 behind a 90-day halt in attacks that Kataib Hezbollah and Nujaba reject; Israeli forces assaulted a shepherd in Quneitra (SANA, single source) after Sharaa said on 22–23 Sep that security talks reached about 90% before Israel pulled back; no new Israel–Syria development was reported on 25 Sep (Arab News, The National, MEMO, Jerusalem Post).

timeline.text: The Houthis declare a naval and air blockade of Saudi Arabia in response to a strike on Sanaa airport, ending four years of relative calm under the 2022 truce.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi says 30 September is the 'fixed and final' date for ending the US-led coalition mission and completing the withdrawal of its forces.
Drones launched from Iraq's Maysan province hit Saudi Arabia's East-West crude pipeline in Riyadh and Medina provinces; Riyadh shuts the line the next day and Brent tops $100.
Houthi forces seize Perim Island and the last stretch of Yemen's Red Sea coast a day after taking Mocha, gaining control of Bab al-Mandab and reiterating a ban on Saudi ships.
The Houthis fire a ballistic missile and drones at Riyadh for the first time in this escalation; Saudi Arabia says it was intercepted as smoke rises near King Khalid airport.

Iraq's prime minister moves militia disarmament to a phased plan ending in June 2027 behind a 90-day halt in attacks, as Syrian President Sharaa says security talks with Israel reached about 90 percent before Israel pulled back.

After the Houthis fire a mixed missile and drone barrage at Jazan, Yanbu, Taif and Riyadh and Saudi Arabia intercepts six ballistic missiles, President Macron announces French soldiers, radars and air-defence systems for the Yanbu terminal and the Makkah pact foreign ministers agree in New York to convene their chiefs of staff.

Yemen's President al-Alimi declares general mobilisation and an amnesty for Houthi defectors as the Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani chiefs of staff meet in Riyadh and agree to integrate defensive capabilities under the Makkah pact.

text: On long-range attack versus layered protection, the Rising · Contested status is borne out. The Houthi salvo of 24 Sep mixed ballistic and cruise missiles with drones across four target sets, Saudi forces reported six ballistic interceptions, and the answer on 25 Sep was institutional rather than kinetic: France's radar and air-defence detachment for Yanbu is still to arrive, and the Makkah-pact chiefs of staff agreed in Riyadh to integrate defensive capabilities without naming a battery or a command. Protection holds over cities, but the terminal now depends on an outside detachment and the pact's military content is unproven. On maritime disruption versus route resilience, the Established · Contested status is confirmed from the land side: government forces held Kahboub for a week and took Jabal Nouman in Lahj on 25 Sep, the Houthi drive for depth behind the coast has stalled, and Bab al-Mandab still saw 27 crossings on 24 Sep. Al-Alimi's general mobilisation on 25 Sep and UNICEF's count of 130,000 displaced show the cost of contesting the overlook rather than the strait itself.

On regional basing versus militia targeting, the Established · Contested status is shifting toward host-nation management: coalition forces sit only at Erbil airport, Iraq's airports closed to Iranian carriers on 25 Sep under US sanctions, not militia pressure, disarmament slides to June 2027, and Israel–Syria talks stay at Sharaa's 90 percent (single source).
